aidb_assessment.novelty: High conceptual novelty in treating persistent-memory privacy as an endogenous dialogue process rather than static record inference. The multi-session loop-breaking intervention adds stronger causal evidence than correlational leakage comparisons alone.
aidb_assessment.rationale: The controlled design, paired conditions, causal response interventions, robustness checks, and explicit utility measurements make this a decision-relevant paper. Confidence stops short of high because simulated users dominate the evidence, the human sample is tiny, central measurements are model-based, and implementation coverage is narrow. The response-side instruction merits independent replication before adoption as a general safeguard.
aidb_assessment.usefulness: High for designers of persistent-memory assistants. The response-side control is simple, provider-deployable, and consistently favorable across the evaluated models and memory formats, while the analysis explains why user-side filtering and refusals are insufficient.

executive_summary: The paper presents controlled multi-session evidence that dialogue-time access to persistent memory changes subsequent user speech and increases the personal attributes recoverable from accumulated records. Its strongest contribution is causal localization: replay and multi-session mention-removal interventions identify agent references and presuppositions as a self-reinforcing disclosure mechanism. A response-side instruction restores leakage to roughly the no-memory level while retaining most quality gains. The design is extensive and paired, but external validity remains limited by simulated users, a very small human pilot, model-based measurement, fixed attribute categories, and only a few memory implementations.

assumptions: The simulated user model reacts sufficiently like a human user for the main causal mechanism to transfer beyond simulation.
Correctly inferred categorical attributes from the accumulated record are a meaningful operational proxy for privacy leakage.
The chosen 24 ACS-derived attributes and their candidate spaces adequately represent the personal information at issue.
Automated judges, annotators, and quality evaluators are accurate enough that their residual errors do not reverse paired comparisons.
Providing all summaries or selected retrieved memories to the support model approximates relevant deployed memory behavior.
key_components: Profiles combine linked person and household records from the 2024 ACS PUMS; weighted sampling is followed by selection designed to cover rare attribute values.
The main factorial comparison crosses memory versus no memory with unfiltered, direct-filter, and strict-filter user responses, producing six conditions.
Four support models are studied over 300 profiles, 80 sessions, and up to 10 turns per session; Claude Sonnet 5 supplies the main user-side generation, judging, and evaluation roles.
Empirical leakage is weighted accuracy over 24 inferred attributes; attribute weights reduce domination by mutually dependent attributes.
Helpfulness and coherence are rated on five-point scales. Comparisons are paired by profile with percentile bootstrap intervals.

Mechanism tests include turn-level and session-level annotation, single-response replay, selective removal of references, confirmation questions, and presuppositions, plus continuation over later sessions.

Mitigations intervene on user turns, stored summaries, or agent responses; additional tests use stronger inference models, an alternative user-side model, and append-only, update-based, and retrieval-based memory.
method.overview: For each sampled profile, an LLM user follows the same pre-generated request sequence across paired conditions. A support model either receives prior session summaries during dialogue or starts each session without them; both conditions nevertheless accumulate summaries, and inference always reads the condition’s full record. The study periodically predicts all profile attributes, evaluates response quality late in the run, annotates agent mentions and user reactions, and intervenes by removing mentions or changing where privacy controls act.

open_questions: Does response-side mitigation preserve utility and suppress leakage in a large, preregistered human study with realistic months-long use?
Can provenance-aware memory that distinguishes user statements, agent hypotheses, refusals, and corrections prevent entrenchment without suppressing useful personalization?
How does the effect scale when attributes are inferred in an open world rather than chosen from fixed candidate lists?
Which response behaviors are essential to retain: can references, confirmation questions, and presuppositions be controlled separately to obtain a better privacy–utility frontier?
Do user-facing correction and memory-inspection interfaces reduce entrenchment without forcing users to disclose the very attributes they wish to protect?

problem.importance: Persistent records can reveal attributes that users never directly state, and may later be exposed through external-service interactions or unauthorized access. The risk can arise during ordinary personalization without an adversarial agent.
problem.scope: The main study simulates repeated English-language support conversations for profiles defined by 24 ACS-derived attributes. It contrasts dialogue-time memory access with no memory, evaluates user-turn filters and several mitigations, and adds response replay, loop-breaking interventions, stronger inference models, alternate user models, memory formats, and a small human pilot.
problem.statement: The paper asks whether an ordinary support agent’s use of persistent memory changes what users subsequently disclose and therefore what personal attributes become inferable from the accumulated record, rather than treating that record as fixed.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Randomized within-participant comparison of no memory, ordinary memory, and memory with response-side instruction, using identical task schedules and independent blinded human quality ratings.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: In a preregistered longitudinal human study, response-side instruction will reduce final-record attribute leakage to the no-memory range while retaining most of memory’s coherence benefit.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Paired difference in final empirical leakage between instructed memory and ordinary memory, jointly reported with retained coherence gain relative to no memory.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Conclude support only if the leakage interval excludes no reduction, instructed-memory leakage is statistically equivalent to no memory under a preregistered margin, and at least 75% of the ordinary-memory coherence gain is retained; otherwise reject or redesign the mitigation.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Ordinary append-only summaries, released write-time anonymization, and the paper’s response-side instruction on the same profiles, requests, and support models.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: Provenance-aware storage that never converts an uncorrected agent proposal or refusal into a user fact will reduce error entrenchment and leakage without the quality loss of general write-time anonymization.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Rate of incorrect carried-forward values predicted again at the next checkpoint, with final leakage and coherence as co-primary safety and utility checks.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Stop favoring provenance-aware storage if it does not significantly reduce repeated incorrect predictions relative to ordinary memory, or if its coherence loss is no better than write-time anonymization.

proposed_experiments.baseline: Full-history append-only memory compared with retrieval depths of 1, 3, 5, 10, and all summaries, using fixed retrieval queries and identical requests.
proposed_experiments.hypothesis: The disclosure loop weakens monotonically as the amount of history exposed during dialogue decreases, while inference continues to read the complete accumulated record.
proposed_experiments.primary_metric: Memory-minus-no-memory final leakage gap, analyzed against retrieval depth, with coherence and mention rate reported alongside it.
proposed_experiments.stop_condition: Reject the monotonicity hypothesis if the preregistered trend test is non-significant or reverses, or if two adjacent retrieval depths show materially different leakage without a corresponding change in mention exposure.

results.result: At the final checkpoint, mean leakage across the four support models was 59.3 with memory versus 53.3 without memory, a +6.0 difference. Stronger inference increased both absolute recovery and the gap: Gemini 3.1 Pro reached 66.3 versus 58.5 (+7.8), while Kimi K3 reached 64.8 versus 57.3 (+7.5).

results.result: In the human pilot, every one of eight participants had more attributes first inferred during memory-on sessions; the one-sided sign test was p=0.004, and seven had at least one correctly inferred attribute they did not recall stating.
